passage_text: Researchers performed a titration experiment to determine the pKa and pI values of glycine, lysine, and aspartic acid. Each amino acid (0.1 M) was dissolved in unbuffered 0.1 M NaCl (background electrolyte). A calibrated NaOH solution (0.1 M) was added in 0.5 mL increments while the pH was recorded after each addition. The resulting titration curves were plotted as pH versus volume of NaOH added. The midpoint of each buffering region (where the pH change per added volume is minimal) was taken as the pKa of the corresponding functional group. The pI was calculated by averaging the pH values at which the net charge of the amino acid is zero. The experiment was repeated three times to assess reproducibility. The data were tabulated and used to validate Henderson–Hasselbalch calculations and to illustrate the influence of ionic strength on acid–base equilibria.
stem: Which variable was manipulated by the researchers during the titration?
explanation: Correct: B) The experimenter chose how much 0.1 M NaOH to add (0.5 mL increments); pH was then recorded in response, so volume of NaOH is the manipulated (independent) variable. Why the others are wrong: A) pH is the measured response. C) Time was not varied as a treatment. D) Temperature was not manipulated.
trap: Choosing pH as the manipulated variable because it is the quantity plotted and recorded most often, when it is the measured response to the NaOH volume added.

stem: If the ionic strength of the solution were increased, what would most likely happen to the apparent pKa of the α‑NH₃⁺ group of glycine?
explanation: Extended Debye–Hückel: pKa′ = pKa + A(2z − 1)√I/(1 + √I), where z is the net charge of the acid form and A ≈ 0.51 at 25 °C. At I = 0.1 M the shift is about ±0.1 pH unit per unit of (2z − 1). For α‑NH₃⁺ the acid form is the zwitterion (net 0, 2z − 1 = −1), so pKa₂′ decreases slightly with ionic strength.
trap: Believing that more salt makes the amine group more acidic or leaves it unchanged; for a zwitterionic acid form (net charge 0) added ions stabilize the charged conjugate base, lowering the apparent pKa slightly rather than raising it or leaving it unchanged.

stem: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, what is the pH when the α‑COOH group of glycine is 50 % neutralized?
explanation: Correct: A) At 50% neutralization of the alpha-carboxyl group [A-]/[HA] = 1, so pH = pKa + log(1) = 2.34. Why the others are wrong: B) 5.97 is the pI, where the net charge is zero, not the carboxyl pKa. C) 9.60 is the pKa of the amino group. D) 7.00 is neutral pH and has no link to this group.
trap: Students may mistakenly use the pI (5.97) instead of the α‑COOH pKa.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the units of a pKa value?

options.A: pKa is expressed in joules per mole (J/mol)
options.B: pKa is expressed in kilocalories per mole (kcal/mol)
options.C: pKa is expressed in moles per liter (mol/L)

explanation: Correct: D) pKa = -log10(Ka) is a logarithm of a ratio of activities, so it is a pure number with no units. Why the others are wrong: A) J/mol would be an energy unit such as the free energy, which is related to pKa but is not pKa itself. B) kcal/mol is likewise an energy unit. C) mol/L is the unit of concentration, not of a negative logarithm.
trap: Confusing pKa with the free energy change or with Ka concentration units; taking the logarithm removes any units, so pKa is dimensionless.

stem: Why is the solubility of a protein usually lowest at its isoelectric point?

options.A: Net charge is zero, so electrostatic repulsion between molecules is minimal and aggregation is favored
options.B: The protein is fully denatured at its pI
options.C: The protein carries maximum positive charge at its pI
options.D: Water cannot hydrate a neutral protein at all

explanation: Correct: A) At the pI the net charge is zero, so repulsion between protein molecules is minimal and aggregation and precipitation are favored. Why the others are wrong: B) The protein is not necessarily denatured at its pI. C) The net charge is zero at the pI, not maximal. D) A neutral protein still has polar surface groups and is hydrated; solubility is lowest, not absent.
trap: Thinking that zero net charge means the protein is denatured or cannot bind water at all; the pI only removes electrostatic repulsion between molecules, so aggregation is favored.
